Google now writes
your story.
Here's how to take it back.

Google is testing AI-generated summaries under paid search ads. For the first time, a paragraph you did not write can sit inside your ad slot and reframe what your business means to a potential customer. This is not a future threat — it is live, spotted July 1, 2026. Here is what the shift means, and exactly what every business should do about it before the rollout reaches them.

// Inspired by Neil Patel

This article expands on an insight from Neil Patel's marketing newsletter — that the new job of marketing is not writing better copy, but creating such strong evidence that AI naturally picks the story you want it to tell. The implementation framework below applies that insight specifically to South African and global SMEs.

// Chapter 01 — What just changed

For 25 years, the deal between businesses and Google was simple. You wrote the copy. Google sent the traffic. Your headline, your benefits, your guarantee — you decided what people saw first, and Google's job was to find the right people and point them at your page.

That deal just changed.

On July 1, 2026, Search Engine Land reported that Google is testing AI-generated summaries that can appear directly beneath paid search ad descriptions. Digital marketer Darcy Burk spotted the test first, posting a screenshot on X — showing a machine-written summary sitting right below the standard Google Ads description, with a disclaimer noting the AI response is generated independently and can make mistakes.

This is not written by the advertiser or approved by them. It is created by Google AI separately from the copy that was actually paid for by the business. You spent money on the ad. You wrote the headline. You chose the offer. And then Google's AI appended its own paragraph — its own interpretation of what your business is — right next to it.

That is new. That is significant. And most businesses have absolutely no plan for it.

"Your copy is no longer the only voice in the ad slot, so it has to say something specific enough that a paraphrase cannot flatten it into the same sentence as everyone else."

Why this is bigger than it looks

// Chapter 02 — The control problem

At first glance, this sounds like a minor UI experiment. A disclaimer is attached. It is a small test. Google has not confirmed a wider rollout. Why should a business owner in Cape Town — or anywhere — care right now?

Because this is not really about ads. The ads test is the visible leading edge of something that is already happening at scale in organic search: AI Overviews now dominate the top of many search results, condensing information from multiple web pages into conversational summaries that often appear before paid and organic listings. Google has been generating its own interpretation of your business for organic results for over a year. Extending this to paid results is the logical next step — not a surprise, and almost certainly a permanent direction.

The control problem is this: if Google's AI decides which parts of your business to highlight in its summary — and it makes that decision based on signals it finds across your website, your reviews, your case studies, your videos, and your listed information — then the business that has systematically shaped those signals controls the narrative. The business that has not, does not.

Maybe you want customers to notice your pricing. Google highlights your turnaround time. Maybe your guarantee is your strongest differentiator. Google talks about your payment terms instead. That is not a hypothetical — it is what happens when the AI has no strong, consistent signal about what your business wants to be known for.

Write better ad copy
Optimise for click-through rate
A/B test headlines
Own the first impression
Control what people see first
New marketing job

The SEO, GEO, and AEO framework — what each one does

// Chapter 03 — Three disciplines, one goal

Most businesses are familiar with SEO. Fewer understand GEO. Almost none have implemented AEO yet. All three are now essential — and the good news is that the same content and infrastructure work serves all three simultaneously.

SEO — Search Engine Optimisation — is still about getting on Page 1 of Google. Core Web Vitals, backlinks, keyword relevance, technical site structure. Nothing has changed here. The fundamentals still work. What has changed is that good SEO is now the floor, not the ceiling. Getting people to your page is step one of a longer journey.

GEO — Generative Engine Optimisation — is about getting AI models to cite your business when users ask relevant questions. When someone asks ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google Gemini "what is the best commission-free accommodation platform in Africa?" — GEO is what determines whether TripSpace Global appears in that answer. It works through structured entity data: a well-built llms.txt file, JSON-LD Schema markup that describes your business clearly to machine readers, a context-ai.txt file that provides grounding information for AI models, and content that explicitly answers the questions your customers are asking.

AEO — Answer Engine Optimisation — is about appearing in AI-generated answers and featured snippets directly. Websites must prioritize AEO, structuring content semantically and building deep topical authority to remain visible in AI Overviews, Gemini, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and other conversational AI systems. AEO is the discipline that determines what AI says about you before someone ever clicks. It is, in the context of Google's new ad summaries, the most directly relevant skill a business can develop right now.

How to shape the story AI tells — the practical framework

// Chapter 04 — Seven actions. No ad spend required.

Everything below costs time and expertise, not budget. This is Neil Patel's core thesis applied practically: you do not need to outspend the competition. You need to out-evidence them. Create such a clear, consistent, well-structured body of proof that AI has no choice but to pick the story you want it to tell.

// Action 01 — Define your one thing
Decide what AI should say about you — before AI does
Before any technical implementation, answer this question: if an AI model generated a single sentence describing your business to a potential customer, what should that sentence say? Not your mission statement. Not your tagline. The sentence that would make someone click rather than scroll past. Write it down. Make it specific. Then build every piece of content and evidence around confirming that sentence. Vague businesses get vague AI summaries. Specific businesses get specific citations.
// Action 02 — Implement JSON-LD Schema on every page
Give AI the structured data it needs to describe you accurately
JSON-LD Schema is machine-readable markup that tells Google and AI models exactly what your business is, what it offers, where it operates, and how to contact it. Most websites have none. A basic implementation takes two hours and immediately improves how AI models describe you. At minimum: Organisation schema, LocalBusiness schema, and FAQPage schema on your main pages. If you sell products: Product schema with reviews. If you publish articles: Article schema with author entity. Each schema type is a structured signal that feeds directly into AI-generated summaries.
// Action 03 — Deploy llms.txt and context-ai.txt
Build files designed specifically for AI crawlers
llms.txt sits at the root of your domain and provides AI models with a structured overview of your business: who you are, what you do, your key claims, your service areas, your differentiators. context-ai.txt provides deeper grounding — the facts, figures, and citations that an AI model should draw on when describing you. Together, these two files are the most direct influence you can have on how AI models describe your business. No other business in your category has them. That is the current opportunity window — and it will not stay open indefinitely.
// Action 04 — Build review volume on the right platforms
Reviews are evidence. AI reads them.
Google's AI summaries pull from the same signals as Google's ranking algorithms — and reviews are one of the strongest. Not just the star rating. The text of the reviews. If your customers consistently describe you using specific language — "fastest turnaround," "no hidden fees," "they actually explained everything" — that language shows up in AI summaries. Ask every satisfied customer to leave a Google review. Coach them gently on what to mention. Not fake reviews. Real customers, prompted to be specific about what they valued. That specificity feeds directly into the story AI tells.
// Action 05 — Publish content that answers specific questions
Content authority is the new domain authority
AI Overviews and AI summaries pull from content that directly answers the questions users are asking. Websites that provide expert analysis, original insights, authoritative content, structured answers, and semantic depth will become more valuable as core AI citation sources. Identify the five questions your customers most often ask before buying. Write a definitive, well-sourced article answering each one. Not keyword-stuffed content. Not AI-generated filler. Genuine expertise in writing, with your specific market knowledge, structured with clear headings and concise answers in the first paragraph. This is the content AI cites. This is the content that shapes the summary.
// Action 06 — Claim and optimise every business listing
AI aggregates. Give it consistent signals to aggregate.
Google pulls business information from Google Business Profile, your website, industry directories, review platforms, and social profiles. Inconsistent information across these sources creates conflicting signals — and AI that cannot confidently describe you, does not describe you. Claim Google Business Profile and fill every field. Ensure your NAP (Name, Address, Phone) is identical across every platform. Add your services, products, hours, and photos. List on relevant directories — Forge Vertical's directory, industry-specific platforms, Cape Town business directories. Each consistent listing is another data point for the AI to draw from.
// Action 07 — Case studies over claims
AI trusts evidence. Give it specific, verifiable proof.
Any business can claim "excellent service" or "industry-leading results." AI is increasingly good at recognising generic claims and discounting them. What AI cannot discount is specific evidence: a case study that describes a real client, a real problem, a real solution, and a real outcome with real numbers. One genuine case study with specific before-and-after figures is worth more to your AI narrative than ten pages of marketing copy. Publish them on your website. Structure them with clear headings. Include the industry, the challenge, and the measurable result. That is the kind of evidence that feeds directly into AI-generated summaries — and that competitors cannot replicate without actually doing the work.

What this means for Forge Vertical clients specifically

// Chapter 05 — Applied to your business

Every website Forge Vertical builds ships with JSON-LD Schema, llms.txt, context-ai.txt, robots.txt with AI crawler permissions, and a structured sitemap — as standard. Not as extras. Not as a premium tier. Standard. This is what infrastructure-first building means in 2026: the technical foundation that positions your business correctly in the AI-generated search landscape is built in from the first line of code, not retrofitted after the fact when the opportunity has already passed to someone who moved earlier.

The content side — the case studies, the question-answering articles, the review strategy, the entity-building editorial calendar — is the part that requires ongoing work. It is the part that no agency can do for you without your expertise, your customer relationships, and your willingness to document what you know. But it is also the part with the highest long-term return, because it compounds. Every article you publish, every review your customers leave, every case study you add to your site increases the body of evidence that AI draws from when it describes you.

The compounding advantage: A business that started building structured AI evidence six months ago is already ahead of one that starts today. A business that starts today is already ahead of one that waits until the Google AI summaries feature rolls out to their campaigns. The window for early-mover advantage in GEO and AEO is still open — but the evidence strongly suggests it will not remain open much longer. The businesses building this infrastructure now are the ones AI will cite next year.

The practical timeline — what to do this week

If you read nothing else in this article, take these three actions in the next seven days:

  • Day 1–2: Write your one defining sentence. Then audit your website — does every page, every heading, every service description confirm that sentence? Fix the ones that don't.
  • Day 3–4: Implement JSON-LD Organisation and LocalBusiness schema on your homepage. Use Google's Rich Results Test to verify it reads correctly. Add FAQPage schema to your most-visited service pages.
  • Day 5–7: Write a plain-text llms.txt at your domain root. Include: who you are, what you offer, where you operate, your three strongest differentiators, and three specific proof points. Then claim or update your Google Business Profile with complete, consistent information.

Those seven days of work will put you ahead of 80% of businesses in your category for AI discoverability. The remaining 20% requires the longer work — the articles, the case studies, the review strategy, the content calendar. But the foundation comes first.

Google is writing your story right now. Whether it is the story you want depends entirely on the evidence you have given it to work with.
